title: The last judgment (CCC 1038–1041)
hookLine: all will be made plain, and God's justice and mercy seen

lines: WHEN DID WE SEE THEE HUNGRY?
cards: "Lord, when did we see thee hungry?" That's the question at the center of a story Jesus tells near the end of Matthew's Gospel, just before the account of his Passion begins.

A king sits on his throne with all the nations gathered before him, and he separates them, the way a shepherd separates sheep from goats. And here's the strange part: both groups ask the same question.
The praised and the sent away are equally surprised. Yesterday was one person meeting Christ alone. Today is the whole human story, all at once, out in the open.

teach.b: Here's the king's answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me."

Christ was there all along, in the hungry, the stranger, the sick, the prisoner, and the people who fed them didn't know it. First, the Catechism says, the last judgment shows what was really going on the whole time.
Second, it's public. At the end of time, after the resurrection of the dead, every person will stand before Christ, and the truth of each life, and its relationship with God, will be laid bare.

teach.h: NOTHING COVERED THAT SHALL NOT BE REVEALED.
teach.b: Jesus says it in Luke: "there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed: nor hid, that shall not be known." Third, it's the whole story, not just one life.
On that day, the Catechism says, people will see the meaning of all of history, and how God's providence led everything toward its end.

It will show that God's justice wins over every injustice his creatures have done, and that his love is stronger than death. Every hidden wrong, every victim nobody listened to, finally seen. Fourth, what it asks for now.
The Catechism reads this teaching as a call to turn toward God while there is time, and quotes Saint Paul: "Behold, now is the acceptable time."
In the Catholic reading, the scene isn't given to frighten people about the end. It's given so they live today as if everything will one day be seen.

how: Catholics profess in the Creed at Mass that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead, and Matthew's scene of the sheep and the goats is among the Gospels read at Mass.

games.q: you're one of the people the king praises. he says you fed him when he was hungry. what do you say?
o: "we knew it was you all along."
"lord, when did we see thee hungry?"
games.why: they're surprised. they never knew. the king answers: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me."

practice: Bring to mind one part of your life you'd rather nobody looked at closely: a habit, a way you talk about someone, a small shortcut. Ask one plain question: if this were made plain tomorrow, would I change it?
If you pray, ask for the courage to live in the open; if you don't, just let the question sit with you.
